title: Impact of chronic dietary red meat, white meat, or non-meat protein on trimethylamine N-oxide metabolism and renal excretion in healthy men and women
authors: Wang Z, Bergeron N, Levison BS, Li XS, Chiu S, Jia X, et al.
followUp: 4 weeks on each of three isocaloric diets
population: Healthy omnivorous adults with normal renal function, 44 men and 69 women, median age 45 years; randomised crossover of red meat, white meat and non-meat protein diets within high- or low-saturated fat arms

result: Carnitine is enriched in red meat; the red meat diet contained 3.8-fold and 7.9-fold more carnitine than the white meat and non-meat diets. After 4 weeks, plasma TMAO rose about threefold on the red meat diet against the white meat or non-meat diets (P < 0.0001), with median absolute increases of 5.9 and 5.7 μM against non-meat and white meat; urine TMAO also rose. Red meat reduced the fractional renal excretion of TMAO (P < 0.05) and increased that of carnitine, γ-butyrobetaine and crotonobetaine. Isotope tracers (n = 13) showed more TMA and TMAO formed from carnitine, not choline, on the red or white meat diet than on the non-meat diet. Saturated fat did not affect TMAO. Plasma TMAO fell within 4 weeks of stopping red meat. The authors state that the direct contribution of TMAO to cardiovascular disease pathogenesis in humans is unclear.
